sf:0a339e6fe9a547298fa95fb846fa927e.d: A wooden anthropoid coffin dating to the late Twenty-fifth or early Twenty-sixth Dynasty. Parts of the coffin are constructed of wood, which is covered by painted textile to provide a smooth surface. Highly decorated with hieroglyphs and depictions of deities. The interior of the lid is decorated with a large image of the goddess Nut. The coffin was originally inscribed for Ankhapakhered, son of Padiese and Tawer, as can mainly be seen with the inscriptions on the interior of the coffin. At an unknown date, perhaps the Ptolemaic Period, the coffin was usurped for a man called Djedher, a Stolist at Akhmim, who was the son of Harsiese (also a Stolist at Akhmim) and Ibity. The usurpations are evident on the exterior of the lid only. The titles might suggest that the coffin was transferred to Akhmim for reuse.

sf:0efe7006beab4e40ae4fbf531b86689d.n: Funerary inscription of Coelia Hagne, a midwife
sf:0efe7006beab4e40ae4fbf531b86689d.d: Funerary inscription of Coelia Hagne, a midwife. Roman, 1st–2nd century CE. Marble, pigment; 23 x 20.5 x 3.3 cm. ID: 0000.00.0869. Coelia Hagne was a midwife ("obstetrix") who lived in the area of Puteoli, on Italy's Bay of Naples, in the 2nd century CE. This monument was dedicated to her by her husband, Marcus. Midwives like Coelia played a vital role in childbirth, childcare, and women's health in Roman society. Often possessing decades of experience, midwives were experts on the health and well-being of babies and their mothers, even though the mortality rate for childbirth was high. Inscription: * Latin: *D(is) M(anibus) / Coeliae Hagne / obs<t>etrici / M(arcus) Ulpius Zosimus / coniugi sanctissim(ae)* * Translation: "To the Shades of the Underworld: for Coelia Hagne, a midwife. Marcus Ulpius Zosimus (made this) for his most pious wife." For more info and links to raw data, see: https://quod.lib.umich.edu/k/kelsey/x-0000.00.0869

sf:0f52b6a1d6c341bc931d7f518fa56ed4.d: Opisthographic inscription from the site of Tarraco (Tarragona, Spain). Fragment of a plaque with an inscription on both sides. The first refers to a statue dedicated by the town of Tarraco to Pompey in 71 BC. In 49 BC, when Julius Caesar called a meeting of the provincial assembly in Tarraco, this statue was removed and the plaque was turned round and carved with a new dedication to P. Mucius Scaevola, Juliu Caesar´s deputy. From the area of the Tarraco Colonial Forum. 329 photos completely processed in Reality Capture. The project was done with the support of the National Archaeological Museum of Tarragona and the Agència Catalana del Patrimoni Cultural. Catalog No. MNAT 5135. Museu Nacional Arqueològic de Tarragona (2019): Tarraco: Exposición de síntesis. Generalitat de Catalunya Publicacions.

sf:1a033fb5704d422886136f1152f038e0.d: Inscription in Arabic located in the Archaeological Park of Carranque (Toledo, Spain). The inscription was made by reusing a large Roman marble column that was carved from a single block of stone. Everything seems to indicate that the marble to carve the column comes from the Eastern Mediterranean. The inscription could be referring to the owner of the column in Islamic times. 3D model made using 52 images in Reality Capture with additional processing in Geomagic Wrap and InstantMeshes.

sf:1b2a5c0545084392b4e2acc9131d9c32.d: A fragmentary Greek inscribed dedication to the Emperor Nero, from the Greek settlement at Fayoum, Egypt. The dedication was organised with the help of a group called the 6470, known from other sources to represent the Greek elite in that region. Also involved in the dedication is a group of men who in their youthhad undergone military training together.

sf:1b60e919a037498586dd5a444b5552be.d: A funerary cone inscribed for the Chief of the Weavers, Iy, whichdates to the first half of the Eighteenth Dynasty (c. 1550–1400 BC). The cone is unusual in that it is prism-shaped rather than the typical cone shape. Additionally, the stamp has a vertical oval frame rather than circular one. The full length of the cone is preserved, which has a deep red colour. There is a large chip near the front of one side. This cone is type 334 of Davies & Macadam. Iy was buried in a tomb adjacent to TT 12 in the Dra' Abu el-Naga' necropolis, which was recently rediscovered by the Djehuti Project directed by José Galán (Galán & Borrego 2006, 200).

sf:1d4d0265a8294ce980c7f4fc83a2a106.d: Basalt stela; on the front is a relief of Antiochus I Epiphanes greeting the nude Herakles-Verethragna as his equal and proferring his right hand in a Dexiosis scene; king shown wearing a belted tunic, cloak, high decorated tiara or kitaris (an adaptation of the Armenian tiara) and, on the right hip, a four-lobed dagger; Herakles-Verethragna carries his club and the skin of the Nemean lion. On the two sides and back, a late Greek inscription referring to cult practices established by Antiochus; in the centre is a hole, illustrating the object's later re-use as an oil-press. Made from 238 photographs, Sony A6000 by Daniel Pett. In gallery scan during opening hours. sf:2d561e7c7c18440bae02d56bac87474a.d: **Collection:** Roman Archeology Dept. **Inv.-No.:** [CAR-S-101](https://www.online.landessammlungen-noe.at/objects/1018884) **Material:** Marble **Dimensions:** 16,3 × 21,2 × 6 cm **Dating:** 3rd century AD Preserved is depiction of the right, clothed foot of a figure (presumably Mithras). To the left of it are the hoof of the bent hind leg of the bull (?) as well as possibly the left foot of another figure (potentially Cautopates). At the right broken edge, the curled end of another depiction can be seen (possibly a scorpion?). On the smooth base surface, remains of three lines of inscription are visible; traces of red paint are preserved in the letters: D(eo) S(oli) [I(nvicto) M(ithrae)]Aur(elius) Mac[. . . . . . . .]v(otum) s(olvit) [l(ibens) m(erito)] To the unconquered sun god Mithras, Aurelius [Mac...?] gladly fulfilled his vow according to merit (of the god). This object was digitized through the 'Kulturerbe digital' program of the Federal Ministry for Arts, Culture, Public Service and Sport.

sf:2d650f570cc345309760f466d99c7610.d: Denarius of Julius Caesar, Roman, 47–46 BCE. Silver; 1.7 cm diameter; 4 grams. ID: 1991.02.0310. This coin depicts Aeneas, a prince of Troy and legendary ancestor of Caesar. At the end of the Trojan War, Aeneas escaped Troy, carrying his elderly father and holding tight to his young son's hand, settling on the coast of Italy, where his descendants would go on to found Rome. Julius Caesar minted this coin, used to pay his troops in his battle against Cato, as a none-too-subtle justification of his claim to power; connecting himself to his royal ancestor Aeneas and the legend of Rome’s founding. Venus, shown on the obverse, was the mother of Aeneas—this made Caesar the descendant of a goddess, adding even more grandeur to his claimed ancestry. For more info and links to raw data, see: https://quod.lib.umich.edu/k/kelsey/x-1991.02.0310

sf:2e3b9c8a84384cf7aeba7648eb6315bb.n: Tombstone of King Casimir IV Jagiellon
sf:2e3b9c8a84384cf7aeba7648eb6315bb.d: **Full name: Tombstone of King Casimir IV Jagiellon (Kazimierz IV Jagiellończyk)** The tomb of King Casimir IV Jagiellon is sculpted in brown-and-red stone mined in Adnet near Salzburg in Austria and only the internal parts of the canopy are sculpted in Piñczów limestone. The tomb is dated with an inscription of 1492 and was signed by two artists. Under the King’s feet there is a house mark (an abstract copyright mark in the form of hand-written strokes used by late-mediaeval craftsmen) and a signature of the principal artist – Veit Stoss, a Nuremberg-based sculptor. His arrival in Kraków became a breakthrough event for local artistic circles. **For more images and further information, visit:** https://muzea.malopolska.pl/en/objects-list/1034 Inventory number: WKW/eIV/01 Localisation of the physical object: Wawel Royal Cathedral in Kraków, Poland **Digitalisation: Regional Digitalisation Lab, Małopolska Institute of Culture in Kraków, Poland; “Virtual Museums of Małopolska” Project**

sf:2f551fe5aa6346878834805787d1dbdf.d: Venus Verticordia White marble; c.1833-38 By John Gibson Inscribed on the tortoise's shell: 'OPVS IOANNIS GIBSON ROMAE' Gibson recorded how the wealthy MP Joseph Neeld (1789 1856) had visited his studio in Rome several times before asking him to carve a 'Venus, nude, but with some drapery modestly arranged without sacrificing too much of the form'. Inspired by Classical prototypes, Gibson showed the Roman goddess of love as an idealised female nude with elegant curves and soft modelling, holding the golden apple, awarded by Paris for her beauty. Although apples are often associated with carnal love, Gibson called his statue Venus Verticordia, or the turner of men's hearts and later recalled how he had > 'endeavoured to give my Venus that spiritual elevation of character which results from purity and sweetness'. https://data.fitzmuseum.cam.ac.uk/id/object/31066

sf:3be28a22aa3d4510afdfad2720f2a998.d: Sarcophagus of Caius Valerius Firminus with inscription in a profiled frame. The size of the sarcophagus was originally designed for a child. However, it seems that one narrow side was deliberately chiseled away to make room for an adult person. 42 x 97 x 60,5 cm; 3rd century AD. *C(aio) Val(erio) Firmino dec(urioni)* *col(oniae) Sav(ariae), (centurioni) coh(ortis) V Luc(ensium)* *Ant(oniniana) Val(eria) Balendina amita* *nepoti pientissimo reli-* *quias condidit.* "To Caius Valerius Firminus, decurion of the colonia Savaria, centurion of the 5th cohort Lucensium Antoniniana, the aunt Valeria Balendina has buried the remains to the righteous nephew." Model: © Landessammlungen Niederösterreich, Niederösterreich 3D

sf:3be13016cdab4397b9100f53c0797542.d: Fragmentary marble capital, measuring 0.22 m in length, 0.12 m in height, and 0.135 m in thickness. On the lower part, within a 0.06 m wide circular frame, it preserves the remains of a Greek inscription. The letters, 0.05–0.06 m high, are regularly and deeply carved. On the upper section, remains of a relief-carved decoration are visible. Six letters of the inscription are still preserved. The piece is dated to the 5th century AD. 3D model made in RealityCapture; total number of images: 296 This work has been carried out in collaboration with Institutul Național al Patrimoniului and thanks to the support of the Muzeul de Istorie Nationala si Arheologie Constanța Cat no.: 19770

sf:3c35b2a1c02e41e7ba5a1398ce1c59c6.d: A granite stela depicting two intertwined serpents, one with beard and a crown with sun disc, the other with double feathers between horns. The figure with the beard is Serapis-Agathodaimon, while the other is Isis-Thermouthis. These deities are guarantors of royal power and the fertility of the land. The bearded serpent is probably a syncretisation of the Agathodaemon of the Greeks who protected the house and was a guarantor of the the fertility of the land. The stela dates to the Roman era (c. 30 BC–395 AD. Purchased by Captain Peter Johnston Saint, one of Sir Henry Wellcome's primary purchasing agents, from the dealer Elias Hatoun in Cairo in 1931. Arabic numbers are written on the back.

sf:3c109bdb6094418f92c30dd0ca0fe660.d: A mummiform shabti moulded from a pale blue-green glazed faience with details added in black paint. The figure is depicted wearing a plain tripartite wig adorned with a seshed headband that is tied at the back. Its arms are crossed over the chest to hold a pair of hoes modelled in low relief, and the facial features are relatively poorly modelled and worn. On the reverse, a rectangular basket with long shoulder straps is clearly outlined in black paint. An inscription in black ink has been added on the front identifying the owner as Ankhesenaset. This specific figurine exhibits notable surface weathering, leaving the vertical inscription column heavily faded (Janes 2016, 227, cat 101; 2012, 193, cat. 104). See also W5021 for a parallel shabti in the collection. The shabtis of Ankhesenaset come from Abydos, North Cemeteries, Cemetery D, tomb 32, which was excavated by the Egypt Exploration Society. They date to the Twenty-second Dynasty (c. 950–730 BC).

sf:4cdf98049e1140a494458c05f307f0f4.d: **Collection:** Prehistory and Historical Archeology Dept. **Inv.-No.:** [UF-22958.18](https://www.online.landessammlungen-noe.at/objects/1117037) **Material:** gold plated silver **Dimensions:** 21 x 18 mm **Dating:** 1250-1400 CE The shield-shaped ring plate features a recessed central field decorated with a left-facing rooster's head above a six-pointed flower. This is surrounded by a raised frame bearing an inscription and a border. The ring band is flat and D-shaped in cross-section, and is attached to the ring plate via cross profiling. An inscription has been identified on the edges of the ring plate which could be described as a 'love inscription'. LIB / ANE / NDE. This object was digitized through the ‘Kulturerbe digital’ program of the Federal Ministry for Arts, Culture, Public Service and Sport.

sf:6c43a7e62c324404ae785875f65a5650.d: A travertine stone slab with an honorary inscription, found in the area around the church San Pancrazio. It is a dedication with the appropriate decree of the decurions (members of the municipal council) to Caius Cesius Apro. The inscription, which can be dated to the Flavian era, documents Caius Cesius Apro's brilliant career, which covered institutional positions in Ponto and in Bithynia and in the province of Sardinia. 70-80 CE **Location:** Museo Antiquarium di Sestino (AR), Tuscany **Inventory Number:** Base 22A This project was done under the authority of the Soprintendenza Archeologia, belle arti e paesaggio per le province di Siena Grosseto e Arezzo in collaboration with Global Digital Heritage and the Municipality of Sestino. For more details click this link https://izi.travel/it/9f1e-antiquarium-di-sestino/i **Scanner**: Artec Leo **Software:** Artec Studio, Geomagic Wrap, ZBrush, XNormal

sf:6c82cb7614bd48fd8d051aeeed738df6.d: Round-topped limestone funerary stela, which dates to the Twenty-sixth Dynasty (c. 664–525 BC). In the lunette, a winged sun disc is located atop two symmetrical wadjet eyes flanking the nefer sign. The main scene depicts three figures on the right (two males and a female) before the mummiform figure of Osiris. Osiris is shown mummiform holding a was-sceptre and standing on the maat-plinth. He is falcon-headed and has a solar disk on his head. The inscription above the offering table confirms his identity as Osiris. Depictions of Osiris with the iconography of Re-Horakhty are known from Abydos during the seventh–sixth centuries BC. A two line inscription, which is much faded, is located below this scene. The decoration of the stela fits best with Type Abydos II G of Munro's classification, which come from the cemetery of Abydos and date to the sixth century BC.

sf:006f313937934403bbbf790aa0315505.d: A wooden mummiform shabti with a tripartite wig and broad wesekh collar dating to the Ramesside Period (c. 1292–1069 BC). Like other New Kingdom shabtis, this one tends to be quite large. It has a black and yellow colour coating, where the remaining paint on this shabti is a black shiny substance with the details picked out in yellow. The black colour is a type of resin. In the past, this shabti has been said to have been inscribed with the title "Chantress of Amun". However, the inscription is largely unreadable. By the New Kingdom, this title—after that of "Mistress of the House"—was the most common title for elite women, who acted as lay priests attached to temples. The wooden surface shows extensive wear and loss of the painted resin layer, exposing the bare timber substrate beneath.

sf:7bae8697a8424ac9b262dc15553ee82f.d: Small fragment of a round-topped stela dating to the Eighteenth Dynasty with only the upper left side preserved. The stela would have had two wadjet eyes flanking hieroglyphs, although only the left eye and the final hieroglyph (a vessel) are preserved. Below this, two figures (facing right) are seated on the left. The male is shown in front holding a scribal palette in his left hand. The column of hieroglyphs above identifies him as the scribe Amenemhat. His wife is depicted behind him with her left arm over his shoulder and her right grasping his right arm. She is identified as Tanetnebu in the hieroglyphs above. Stelae such as this typically depict an officiant libating in front of the deceased, with a table of offerings between them. The column of hieroglyphs to the right of the male's name identifies the officiant as "his son", although his name has not survived. Previously part of the Kent collection, which was bequeathed to Harrogate Museum in 1968.

sf:7dcbf338b12f45f8a2dbeb3aed8a55ae.d: Cuneiform economic text. Baked clay. Early Bronze Age (Ur III). 1911.10.160. This tablet documents the delivery of leather footwear, including many which were dyed using an imported greenish-blue pigment. These boots and sandals were valued enough to be given as gifts to important foreign dignitaries. sf:7dd9afe2a7b540c9bc488d98e877fdf9.un: Harvard Museum of the Ancient Near East
sf:7dd9afe2a7b540c9bc488d98e877fdf9.d: Funerary Cone of Inhermose (tomb undiscovered) Probably from Thebes, New Kingdom, Dynasty 18 Harvard Semitic Museum 2000.5.3 Funerary cones (small cones made from clay) were placed over the entrance of the chapel of a tomb, forming a sort of frieze. Common in the New Kingdom, they were inscribed with the title and name of the tomb owner, often with a short prayer. The exact purpose of the cones is unknown. “Revered one before Osiris, scribe of the works in the temple of Amunhotep III in the west of Thebes, Inhermose, justified before the great god.” *Scanned by Andrea Martinez on the Artec Spider 3D Scanner*

sf:7f169ca736c949a8a7901376f1ccc582.d: Fragment of inscription of a chief magistrate. Roman, Flavian (69–96 CE). Marble, plaster, pigment; 29.4 x 23.8 x 5.6 cm. ID: 0000.00.0818c. Portion of a larger monumental public inscription. This fragment preserves one complete letter and two partial letters from the middle of the honoree's nomen (family/clan name). Inscription: * Latin: *A(ulus) Caeci(lius Ru)fus II vir*. * Translation: "Aulus Caecilius Rufus, the chief magistrate (*duumvir*)." Chisel marks are visible on the surface of the stone, revealing how it was first roughed out with toothed chisels before being worked more carefully with finer tools; apparently the first pass went a bit too deep on this inscription! The break on this stone connects with other pieces in our collection. For more info and links to raw data, see: https://quod.lib.umich.edu/k/kelsey/x-0000.00.0818c

sf:8b8b94a7b85c4b3aa5b7d031ccd6cf0d.d: Funerary inscription of Callityche, a chamber attendant. Roman, Early 1st century CE. Marble, pigment; 29.5 x 18.4 x 5.5 cm. ID: 0000.00.1030. Callityche was a hairdresser ("ornatrix") from the town of Puteoli on the Bay of Naples, in Italy. She was formerly enslaved by Aulus and Gaia Valerius. We don't know if Callityche, which means "good luck" in Greek, was her actual name or a name assigned to her by her former enslavers. Inscription: * Latin: *Valeria A(uli) et ((C))(aiae) liberta / Callityche / ornatrix* * Translation: "Valeria Callityche, the freedwoman of Aulus and Gaia. A hairdresser." For more info and links to raw data, see: https://quod.lib.umich.edu/k/kelsey/x-0000.00.1030

sf:8d25d6c7ee3141d2a85ed77f0596475e.n: Stećak no. 11, Radimlja near Stolac, BiH
sf:8d25d6c7ee3141d2a85ed77f0596475e.d: Child's gabled roof stećak with inscription. Richly decorated. On one fornt side there is a figure of man with their arm held aloft. The epitaph on the gable suggests that this is a tombstone of Radoje Vuković, the son of Vuk Stipanović, the nephew of good Radoje and voivoda Petar, who erected the monument (+ I God's servant Radoe Vuković nephew of voivoda Petar). There are also two engraved initials B.B. on the fornt side of stećak, next to the figure of a man. Other decorative motives on the monument include arcades with pillars and arches and twisted rope. 3D model made in Reality Capture using 557 images. Additional processing completed in Geomagic Wrap. We want to show our gratitude to Public institution for development of tourism and protection of cultural-historical and natural heritage “Radimlja” Stolac as well as Professor Edin Bujak from the University of Sarajevo.

sf:9a5521bd0ec64d8a91e747a38449312f.n: Funerary inscription of a young boy
sf:9a5521bd0ec64d8a91e747a38449312f.d: Funerary inscription of a young boy, Marcus Valerius Laos. Roman, Late 2nd–early 3rd century CE. Marble, pigment; 30 x 22 x 3.5 cm. ID: 0000.00.1039. Marcus Valerius Laos went by the nickname 'Africanus'. He grew up in Puteoli, a port town in Italy, but his nickname suggests that his family moved there around the time of his birth from the Roman province of Africa. Marcus was only six years old when he died. Translation: "To the Shades of the Underworld: to Marcus Valerius Laos, who (was) also (called) Africanus, dearest son and most dutiful to me beyond other loved ones, who lived for six years, seven days, and three hours. Aurelia Lais, (his) mother, made (this) for her most-beloved, well-deserving son." For more info and links to raw data, see: https://quod.lib.umich.edu/k/kelsey/x-0000.00.1039

sf:9d72b640ae254ada94111904b4c793b7.d: Large sandstone stela likely dating to the Ptolemaic Period (c. 332–30 BC). The stone used for the stela has been reused from an earlier monument, as is evident from the traces of hieroglyphs present on the base. The content of the stela has been divided into three registers, with decoration in sunk relief. In the lunette is a winged sun disk, representing the god Behdety, with pendant uraei. The lunette is separated from the central scene by a sky sign. In this scene is a recumbent bull, facing right, before an offering table. While unlabelled, the bull wears a headdress consisting of a solar disk with double plumes, which is associated with the god Montu (Buchis) at Armant. Behind the bull is a winged solar disk with a single pendant uraeus. The lower register consists of three lines of a demotic text, which mentions Psenmont, son of Psenmont. The personal names Psenmont, which evokes the god Montu, also suggests that Armant is the provenance for this stela. The reverse of the stela is roughly cut.

sf:9d87aac4263347a2aead383b38f47a39.d: Brick stamp LEG (io) XIIII G (emina) of the 14th Roman Legion. The stay in Carnuntum can be proven from 114 AD to the end of the 4th century. Stamp: 10,2 x 5 cm. During this time it was customary to have the building material produced by the soldiers for the erection of a camp. If suitable clay deposits were available, legions operated their own brickyard and stamped their products. Model: © Landessammlungen Niederösterreich, Niederösterreich 3D

sf:009faf2d52b141f8aa4593e688346f9c.n: Stela Dedicated to Ptah by Penmennefer
sf:009faf2d52b141f8aa4593e688346f9c.d: Stele dedicata da Penmennefer a Ptah Stela Dedicated to Ptah by Penmennefer Ptah is one of the oldest gods in the Egyptian pantheon. Patron of craftsmen, Ptah is considered the creator god and ‘sculptor of the earth’. He had a particularly cherished cult at Deir el-Medina and is depicted as a standing figure, covered in a shroud, with his feet placed together, while holding the was sceptre; he usually wears a shrouded headdress and has a straight beard. * **Inv. no.:** S.6139 * **Material:** Stone / Limestone * **Dimensions:** 13 cm x 16 cm x 4.5 cm * **Date:** 1292–1076 BCE * **Period:** New Kingdom * **Dynasty:** Nineteenth – Twentieth Dynasty * **Provenance:** Deir el-Medina * **Acquisition**: Excavation Ernesto Schiaparelli, 1905 https://collezioni.museoegizio.it/en-GB/material/S_6139 https://collezioni.museoegizio.it/it-IT/material/S_6139

sf:9fb5b6cf1a8643fdbb087fc0a6cb26ab.n: Inscription - Church of San Juan Bautista
sf:9fb5b6cf1a8643fdbb087fc0a6cb26ab.d: Inscription preserved on the main portal of access to the medieval Church of San Juan Bautista in Jodra del Pinar (Guadalajara, Spain). This small medieval church was built around 1200 in Romanesque style. The access portal preserves on one side an inscription written in Latin with medieval letters that says: SAN(C) T(E) IOANNES(S) … + BEN(E)DICTUS Q(UI) UENIT I(N) NOMINE DOMINI, that is, "Saint John" + "Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord." We want to publicly thank the collaboration of the Diocesan Delegation of Cultural Heritage of Guadalajara, especially by its cultural delegate Mr. Miguel Ángel Ortega Canales, for the facilities they have given us and for the interest they have shown in the project at all times. SALGADO PANTOJA, José Arturo (2014): Pórticos románicos en las tierras de Castilla. Aguilar de Campoo, Fundación Santa María la Real.

sf:47ababa2dd594379861de66212426d13.d: A figured ostracon consisting of a dynamic sketch executed in red and brown pigments upon the relatively flat surface of a limestone sherd. The upper register depicts a standing cow, a zoomorphic manifestation of the goddess Hathor, identifiable by the sacred solar disc nestled between her long, curved horns. Beneath the divine animal is a lower register showing a procession of figures with their arms raised in the traditional gesture of adoration or praise. The lines of the sketch are delicately applied but weathered, with some fading evident across the lower figures. The reverse of the limestone flake is unworked and features a handwritten notation in blue pencil indicating that the object originates from Deir el-Medina. sf:53e806d433934a8aabec57846d651742.d: A round-topped sandstone stela erected in memory of a sacred cow, the mother of the Buchis Bull. Carved beneath a winged sun disc, the central scene depicts the mummified, crowned cow on a pedestal. The goddess Isis stands before her, acting as an intermediary for the Roman Emperor Commodus (AD 180–192), who offers incense and a water libation over an altar. Five lines of hieroglyphs record the funerary dedication. Dating to AD 190/1, this monument was excavated by the Egypt Exploration Society at Armant, tomb 28 of the Baqaria catacomb where these divine mothers were buried.

sf:68ba9abd86ea4491918e7b9e6949cb9e.n: Humility Brings Prosperity gate - point cloud
sf:68ba9abd86ea4491918e7b9e6949cb9e.d: A big point cloud of the Humility Brings Prosperity gate, now installed in Gallery 200 at Mia. *The gate comes from Shanxi province, which, because of its dry climate, contains the largest concentration of surviving historic wooden structures in China. An inscription on the main beam dates the gate to 1858, during the Qing dynasty (1644–1912).* [More info](https://collections.artsmia.org/art/127331/humility-brings-prosperity-gate-china) *This imposing gate once formed the entrance to the main courtyard of an urban middle-class family compound. The four-character panel over the doorway reads, Humility Brings Prosperity (Lüqian Jianfeng 履謙漸豐). The gate demonstrates the hallmarks of traditional Chinese architecture: a post-and-lintel structure that supports a graceful gable roof and intricate rafters, as well as brackets that extend the eaves and provide decoration. Like other works of traditional Chinese architecture, no glue or nails were used, and the gate was assembled using only joinery and wooden pins.*

sf:77c3af8364b3475eb11ccd162e78714a.d: Inscription located in the Archaeological Park of Carranque (Toledo, Spain), on one of the Roman columns preserved inside a large monumental building that has been interpreted as a Palace (Palatium). Numerous inscriptions in Latin and Greek have been identified on the building's columns, the interpretation of which is still the subject of debate among experts. These inscriptions were made on large 4 meter high Roman marble columns that were carved from a single block of stone. Everything seems to indicate that the marble to carve the columns comes from the Eastern Mediterranean. 3D model was made in Reality Capture using 15 images. Additional processing was completed in Geomagic Wrap and Meshlab

sf:86a3395754b14fefb921e3e42ca49e14.d: Neo-Assyrian clay tablet: containing a dated parivate contract, written in cuneiform, for the sale of a house by Sharru-lu-dari. The tablet has been impressed three times on obverse, between ruled lines 3 and 4, with a conoid or perhaps scaraboid seal. The impression shows a robed worshipper with both hands raised, standing facing left towards a star and crescent. The seal was chipped, both below the crescent and behind the worshipper, where there are traces of some other symbol. COL: https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/W_K-311 Made by Daniel Pett from 301 photographs taken by Terhi Nurmikko-Fuller, ANU.

sf:96f9ae59a49b4a70a0c9b961602efcab.d: An inscribed oracle bone (jia gu 甲骨) from the Couling-Chalfant collection at the British Library. Oracle bones were animal bones, usually ox shoulder bones or the underside of turtle shells, used for divination rituals in ancient China. Dating to the Shang dynasty (c. 1600 – 1050 BC), they bear the earliest extant form of Chinese writing and are the oldest items held in the British Library. The inscription on the reverse of this particular bone records a lunar eclipse, which can be precisely dated to the night of 27 December 1192 BC. This model was created for a British Library project on oracle bones that formed part of the UK-China Cultural Exchange 2015, supported by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport. For more information see: * http://www.bl.uk/collection-items/chinese-oracle-bone#sthash.8cDMmsmE.dpuf * http://britishlibrary.typepad.co.uk/asian-and-african/ Photography: Neil McCowlen Modelling: [Adi Keinan-Schoonbaert](https://sketchfab.com/adiks)

sf:96ffa0eb37ba479693fabcd6cd43acbc.d: "1st century BC - 1st century AD. copper Tetradrachm (12g.)– Obverse: smooth and lightly rounded side. – Reverse: extremely schematic representation of Shamash sitting on the left on a stool, with paralleled legs. In his left hand he holds a long sceptre and in his right hand an eagle . On the right side, vertically few spears and a ring recalling a (Greek?) inscription. Behind the head of the character, a ring. In front of him, on the left side, a big south-Arabic shin." Pre-Islamic , Mleiha, Sharjah, UAE. On display in the Sharjah Archaeology Authority. 1st C CE. Catalog number unk. Processed in Reality Capture from 174 images.

sf:99eab9ab2e6b47e48dbbcaee3d150a91.d: **Collection:** Roman Archeology Dept. **Inv.-No.:** [CAR-K-468](https://www.online.landessammlungen-noe.at/objects/1306844) **Material:** Ceramic **Dimensions:** 10,2 × 8 × 3,6 cm **Dating:** 3rd century AD Wedding Lamp Oval, roughly shaped lamp, with a handle stud on the steep shoulders. Wide, high ridge, leading into a short nozzle, concave discus, a raised ring around the filling hole, with an inscription running around the filling hole on the discus: ECCIPE PATR(one) VE(nerius?) NVB(e) – "Take, Lord Venerius, marry!", retrograde; thin relief letters influenced by italic script; readable outward, with the "O" from "Patrone" omitted from the beginning. Slanted, curved wall, base and surface smoothed, clay strongly glowing. This object was digitized through the 'Kulturerbe digital' program of the Federal Ministry for Arts, Culture, Public Service and Sport.

sf:445e0cd1a8134f3bb6ab5f23e8a05f37.d: The upper portion of a limestone mummiform shabti dating to the early Eighteenth Dynasty (c. 1550–1400 BC). The fragment preserves a detailed upper torso and head, carved from a fine-grained, light-coloured limestone. The figure features a voluminous, unstriated tripartite wig with broad, flat lappets that frame a rounded face with prominent, well-modelled ears. The hands are concealed beneath the smooth, mummiform shroud without any visible agricultural tools. The incised inscription of Chapter 6 of the Book of the Dead begins immediately below the plain chest area, arranged into four remaining horizontal registers that wrap around the front and sides of the body, bounded by deeply carved incised lines. The name of the owner is not clear. The reverse of the figurine remains flat and unincised, showing the straight-cut edge of the back of the wig.

sf:575a1e4345fe46eba33cce7902689aeb.d: Completely preserved roman casserole made of silver. On the disc handle is the inscription DIAN(E). sf:915d128d71494d1687966f26b588afa0.d: A fragment of a funerary stela made from pink alabaster. It depicts the head of the owner and has a partial horizontal inscription above it. The head has stylised features, and the inscription identifies the owner as "Sharah, son of (the clan) [...]". It possibly dates to the first century BC. This fragment is one of three Old South Arabian objects in the collection. Although its exact provenance is unknown, it is likely from the cemetery at Qataban (modern Yemen), given its close stylistic parallel to a stela housed in the National Museum of Yemen, Sana'a (YM 69). Such stelae were used as grave markers. Purchased at auction by Sir Henry Wellcome in 1931 (lot 71). On long-term loan to the Egypt Centre since 1971 as part of the dispersal of the Wellcome collection.

sf:2015b78ea2784fbb8f3abf146b3cd12f.d: A wooden footboard from a cartonnage case with a black bull. It is painted red on black. The bull wears a menat collar. The inscription above reads "Osiris Apis". The Apis Bull was added to the decoration of private coffins and cartonnages from the Twenty-second Dynasty onwards. The object dates to the Third Intermediate Period (c. 1069–715 BC). Purchased by Sir Henry Wellcome in 1924 from the collection of the Reverend Frankland Hood (lot 138). According to the auction catalogue, much of Hood's collection came from Thebes. On loan to the Egypt Centre since 1971 as part of the distribution of the Wellcome collection.

sf:3694cbcc6ae34741ad96109b619d4d52.d: Tetradrachm with the head of Alexander the Great with Ammon's horn and diadem looking to the right. On the reverse, Athena Nikephoros sits in armor with shield and spear. Athena's nickname "Nikephoros" comes from the fact that she is depicted here with the goddess Nike on her outstretched right hand. In the left-hand field of the coin in front of the goddess is the letter M. The coin inscription reads BAΣIΛEΩΣ ΛYΣIMAXOY. Although Alexander the Great is depicted, according to the inscription, King Lysimachus was the mint master. Lysimachus was a general of Alexander the Great and one of the Diadochi after his death. Silver; dm 2,9 cm; 306-281 BC. Tetradrachme des Lysimachos für Alexander dem Großen. Auf der Vorderseite Kopf Alexander des Großen mit Ammonshorn und Diadem nach rechts blickend. Auf der Rückseite sitzt Athena Nikephoros in Rüstung mit Schild und Speer mit der Göttin Nike auf ihre ausgestreckten, rechten Hand. Silber; Dm 2,9 cm; 306-281 v. Chr.

sf:22897d51cc014e6f9aee76cbcfa2028b.d: A base dedicated to Emperor Antoninus Pius, who reigned from 138 to 161 CE. The dedication to Antoninus Pius, which can be dated to after his death, has a fragment of stone added to it with the inscription ALIM[---] which came from the Sestino baths and confirms how the municipality successfully obtained funds from the Institutio alimentaria. **Location:** Museo Antiquarium di Sestino (AR), Tuscany **Inventory Number:** Base 6 This project was done under the authority of the Soprintendenza Archeologia, belle arti e paesaggio per le province di Siena Grosseto e Arezzo in collaboration with Global Digital Heritage and the Municipality of Sestino. sf:33770f982b5f4a5f8abd836ad0327f4f.d: Round-topped limestone funerary stela with incised decoration dating to the Thirteenth Dynasty (c. 1803–1649 BC). The decoration is divided into three registers, all of which are surrounded by a thin incised border. In the upper lunette are two large wadjet eyes. Previous restoration work is visible just below the eyes. The second register consists of three lines of hieroglyphs, to be read from right to left, containing the offering formula addressed to Osiris. In the lower register, two figures are shown standing and facing each other. A large table of offerings is located between them. On the left is a male figure, who holds a lotus blossom in his left hand while his right arm is pendant. He wears a kilt with a projecting apron. The inscription identifies him as Iwefenirpeseshi. Opposite him is his mother, wearing a long dress with a single strap over the shoulder. She holds a duck by the head in her right hand while her left arm is pendant. The hieroglyphs in front of her face identify her as Neferhotep.

sf:79859a4ef198428385836d222d9c4e96.n: Roman funeral monument of Mercator, Evora
sf:79859a4ef198428385836d222d9c4e96.d: Roman funeral monument of gray marble dated between the year 151 A.D. and 210 A.D. It belonged to Mercator. In the inscription that still retains on one of its faces we can read: D(is). M(anibus). S(acrum). MERCATOR ANN(orum) XXXII (triginta duorum) VXOR. MARITO MERENTI. POSVIT H(ic). S(itus). E(st). S(it).T(ibi). T(erra). L(evis). The translation according to Encarnação, (1984) would say: “Consecrated to the Manes gods. Here lies Mercator, thirty-two years old. The wife of the deserved husband put. May the earth be light to you”. Mercator could be a slave. The funerary monument is of the Cupa type. It is currently preserved in the Frei Manuel do Cenáculo National Museum (Évora, Portugal). Catalog No. ME1822. ENCARNAÇÃO, José d' - IRCP - Inscrições Romanas do Conventus Pacensis - Subsídios para o estudo da romanização. Coimbra: Inst. Arqueolog. Fac. Letras, 1984, pp. 386-7,767,771. 669 photos from Canon 5D Mk IV. Completely processed in Reality Capture.

sf:380056e846df4ffbb9ccacbfc80b7327.d: A low-res version of the Humility Brings Prosperity gate, now installed in Gallery 200 at Mia. The gate comes from Shanxi province, which, because of its dry climate, contains the largest concentration of surviving historic wooden structures in China. An inscription on the main beam dates the gate to 1858, during the Qing dynasty (1644–1912). [More info](https://collections.artsmia.org/art/127331/humility-brings-prosperity-gate-china) *This imposing gate once formed the entrance to the main courtyard of an urban middle-class family compound. The four-character panel over the doorway reads, Humility Brings Prosperity (Lüqian Jianfeng 履謙漸豐). The gate demonstrates the hallmarks of traditional Chinese architecture: a post-and-lintel structure that supports a graceful gable roof and intricate rafters, as well as brackets that extend the eaves and provide decoration. Like other works of traditional Chinese architecture, no glue or nails were used, and the gate was assembled using only joinery and wooden pins.*

sf:88357751196f4a4883023876dea15288.d: Travertine slab with a dedication to Titus, emperor of the Flavian dynasty who ruled from 79 to 81 CE. Titus distinguished himself as a general for his repression of the revolt in Judea in 70 CE. His participation, using his own wealth, in the repairs to the damage suffered by Pompeii and Herculaneum following the 79 CE eruption earned him the definition “delight and darling of the human race” by the historian Suetonius. The inscription is datable to 73 CE, when Titus assumed the position of caesar. **Location:** Museo Antiquarium di Sestino (AR), Tuscany **Inventory Number:** Panel 3 This project was done under the authority of the Soprintendenza Archeologia, belle arti e paesaggio per le province di Siena Grosseto e Arezzo in collaboration with Global Digital Heritage and the Municipality of Sestino. sf:a7b5a2430107486b998489514eb25ec3.d: Roman thymiaterion with dedication inscription. The incense bowl with serrated rim stands on an altar-shaped base with half-plastic eagles at its corners. The support ring for the bowl is carried by four dolphins pointing downward. The altar shaft is inscribed with the dedicatory inscription of Lucius Messius, a benefactor from the staff of the governor, addressed to "Dominus". Consecrations to Dominus (often accompanied by Domina) are known several times from Dacia and Pannonia, as well as from an altar from Carnuntum. Bronze; h 22,1 cm; dm 18,5 cm Do/mi(no) / f(ier)i / ut pact/us / ius(s)it v/isu L(ucium) M/es(s)ium / m(ilitem) / b(eneficiarium) co(n)s(ularis) / legio(nis) "To make it (i.e., this bronze) to the Lord, as he (i.e., the god) had agreed, he commanded by means of a dream Lucius Messius, the soldier, beneficiarius consularis of the legion." Model: © Landessammlungen Niederösterreich, Niederösterreich 3D

sf:a8176d5e9c994343a8800453e8769905.d: Limestone male figurine ([GR.239.1888](https://data.fitzmuseum.cam.ac.uk/id/object/66385)) with mantle and inscription found in Amargetti Cyprus, dating from 300 B.C. — 201 B.C. The statue is schematically-carved with an important dedicatory inscription engraved at the back referring to a dedication on behalf of [...] to Opaon Melanthios, a god of the shepherds. This god is often identified with the god Pan, who had a sanctuary at Amargetti in the Paphos District of Cyprus, where this statue was found. This 3D model was made as part of the [#CEEF3D project](http://creative-economy.fitzmuseum.cam.ac.uk/) at the Fitzwilliam Museum, in connection to [Being an Islander: Art and Identity of the large Mediterranean Islands](http://www.fitzmuseum.cam.ac.uk/being-islander-art-and-identity-large-mediterranean-islands).

sf:a8942c5f5ad94a5ca132e6b6fc33dad1.d: The shield (*tas*) is one of the elements of the ritual “outfit” of the synagogue Torah scroll (*klej kodesz*). Rectangular, closed with a trifoliate arch, with the figures of Moses (on the left) and Aaron (on the right), and the Tablets of Stone (in the middle), with the initial words of the Ten Commandments engraved in Hebrew. The figures of Moses and Aaron are flanked by spiral columns. On their plinths there are Hebrew inscriptions marking the date. In the three-leaf top, three openwork crowns with colourful glasses are attached. Between the crowns, on the plaque with floral motifs, there is an engraving of the Tetragrammaton. **For more images and further information, visit:** https://muzea.malopolska.pl/en/objects-list/552 Inventory number: MHK 282/VII Localisation of the physical object: Museum of Kraków, Poland **Digitalisation: Regional Digitalisation Lab, Małopolska Institute of Culture in Kraków, Poland; “Virtual Museums of Małopolska” project**

sf:b8d3e1125b63456085ed0c2b82b7ae52.n: Bilingual inscription Tomb FA-5, Mleiha, Sharjah
sf:b8d3e1125b63456085ed0c2b82b7ae52.d: Bilingual South-Arabian / Aramaic funerary inscription discovered inside the burial chamber of tomb FA-5, Mleiha, Sharjah, UAE. (Overlaet 2018:14 Figure 9, Catalog No. 1). Central panel in south Arabian script, text along the rim in Aramaic. Text reads “Memorial and tomb of Amud son of Gurr son of Ali, inspector of the king of Oman, which built over him his son Amud son of Amud son if Gurr, inspector of the king of Oman.” Dated to either 222/221 or 215/214 BCE. First record evidence of an Oman Kingdom (Overlaet 2018:13). Model of the cast of the original before restoration. 358 photos. Completely processed (aligned, scaled, modeled, cleaned, simplified, unwrapped, textured, meshed) in Reality Capture. B. Overlaet 2018. Mleiha, An Arab Kingdom on the Caravan Trails (Brussels 30.10-30.12.2018). Sharjah: Sharjah Archaeology Authority.

sf:b31e2b52f99e4c2faaf8ec17ae1c4d16.d: The upper right corner of a round-topped limestone stela dating to the Eighteenth Dynasty. On the far right, a man is depicted with his arms raised in adoration. He wears a pleated dress and a wig with curls. The hieroglyphs above his head describe him as adoring and praising Amun, while the column in front identifies him as a scribe. Unfortunately, his name is not preserved. The thicker column in the centre of the stela presents the name and titles of the god Amun-Re, who must have been depicted on the left of the stela. Both occurrences of the name Amun have been erased, a clear indication that this stela dates to before the reign of Akhenaten in the Eighteenth Dynasty.

sf:b90c008d8c1e43c0a2d2a310674f1a13.d: A wooden footboard from a cartonnage case with a black and white Apis Bull painted upon it. The Apis bull wears a uraeus on his head and a red beaded net on his back. The inscription around the bull identifies it as the Apis. It also states that the object was made for the Mistress of the House and Chantress of Amun, Tjesmutperet, daughter of Nespasefy. Anubis is written on the back of the board in black. The Apis Bull was added to the decoration of private coffins and cartonnages from the Twenty-second Dynasty onwards. The object dates to the Third Intermediate Period (c. 1069–715 BC). Part of the collection of Sir Henry Wellcome. On loan to the Egypt Centre since 1971 as part of the distribution of the Wellcome collection.

sf:b300b5f7bfde46fd97d7c15ef25bd07c.d: Round-topped limestone funerary stela, which dates to the Twenty-sixth Dynasty (c. 664–525 BC). The decoration on the front face has been added in black ink, with some traces of red ink for some of the internal details. In the lunette, a winged sun disc is located atop two symmetrical wadjet eyes. In the scene below, two figures (female and male) are shown on the right with their arms raised in adoration before the mummiform figure of Osiris. The lower half of an additional figure, perhaps Isis, is depicted behind Osiris. Beneath the main scene are two horizontal lines of hieroglyphs, which possibly begins with an offering formula addressed to Osiris. Unfortunately, the second like, which would have contained the name of the deceased, is unreadable. The condition of the stela is relatively poor, which has been blackened by dirt and grime. The decoration of the stela fits best with Type Abydos II G of Munro's classification, which come from the cemetery of Abydos and date to the sixth century BC.

sf:b461baf4969745d0b0ab7117d556b4e5.d: Latin verse inscription in highlighted red letters on grey sandstone recording the visit of Mamertinus, Roman governor of Egypt, to the singing statue of Memnon at Thebes. The author praises the piety of the age of Hadrian which caused the statue to sing. Made by [Daniel Pett](https://sketchfab.com/danielpett) from 37 OnePlus3 mobile phone photographs. This is attached to the wall in gallery 70, so the reverse and base is not visible fully for photogrammetry. COL: [GAA1852](https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/G_1973-0107-1)

sf:b511b0889a014430b2252f6f68880ebe.d: A wooden funerary stela, which dates to the Ptolemaic Period (c. 332–30 BC). It contains painted decoration on the front face. The upper register shows the winged sun disc representing Horus of Edfu (Behdety). Two uraei hang down from the sun disc, each of whom wears the Red Crown (right) and White Crown (left). Between the uraei are the rays of the sun, which are painted red. The upper scene is separated from the central one by the sign for the sky. In this register, the deceased is depicted on the right with his hands raised in adoration before Re and Osiris. A large table of offerings is located between the deceased and the deities, both of whom are represented seated. Re has the head of a falcon and holds an ankh and was-sceptre. Osiris wears the Atef Crown and also holds an ankh and was-sceptre. The final register contains four rows of hieroglyphs painted black, which begin with the offering formula to Re-Horakhty. The inscription identifies the owner as Pamenes, the son of Herefernit and Satweret.

sf:b795363bc5194815a5e05c6202a5a0d6.d: A wooden face, carved in high relief, which was originally part of an anthropoid coffin lid. The timber is largely left in its natural state, devoid of the gesso and polychrome layers seen on more elaborate contemporary examples. The only remaining pigment is found on the eyes, which are simply rendered in black to define the iris and pupil. A rounded headdress sits low across the forehead, carved as an integral part of the wooden block. The reverse side contains an archival inscription reading "Asyut," identifying the geographic origin of the piece. The object features a large, singular mounting hole at the chin and an additional attachment point on the upper portion of the head, which were used to secure the face to the main coffin structure. It likely dates to the Third Intermediate Period (c. 1069–715 BC).

sf:bce70786aead412693b7bca967142099.d: Roman neck ring with inscription. The neck ring shows a piston-shaped enlargement and a cut-out hole of identical shape at the left end. The rims of the obverse are lined with short notches and small punched circles as well as cube eyes in the area of the thickening. Stamped inscription FELICES TVN(GRI) on the obverse and name VRBICVS incised in cursive on the reverse. Torques, originally the neck rings of Celtic warriors, are documented as military awards in the Roman army since Republican times and were usually worn over the breast on the armour. Golden neck rings are also mentioned as a common accoutrement of the draconiarii, the bearers of the Draco standard, which was used as a cohort field sign until late antiquity. The inscription FELICES TUN(GRI) probably refers to the auxiliary unit of the Sagittarii Tungri mentioned in the Notitia dignitatum. It is therefore probably the only military insignia of a standard bearer known at present. Gold; l 8,5 cm; w 1,2–2,4 cm; early 4th century AD.

sf:ca42e593d8aa4b2894dc2b288f595af5.d: Sculpture of a Roman gladiator **A 3D model of an eighteenth-century bronze sculpture created by Pius Weloński (1849–1931).** This figurative, whole-body sculpture depicts a Roman gladiator with an upraised arm. The pedestal bears the following inscription: Ave Caesar! Morituri, salutant [Long live Caesar! Those who are going to die greet you]. The gladiator is – judging by his props – most likely a retiarius [net-fighter]. He fought with a trident or harpoon made of tuna bones, a dagger, and a net that he threw at his opponent’s head. **For more images and further information, visit**: https://muzea.malopolska.pl/en/objects-list/21 Inventory number: MNK II-rz-340 Location of the physical object: National Museum in Kraków, Poland **Digitalisation: Regional Digitalisation Lab, Małopolska Institute of Culture in Kraków, Poland; “Virtual Museums of Małopolska” project.** Project Visualization (3D model + textures): Marcin Solarz

sf:cc588f678717414099658cf485004d81.d: Milestone from the site of El Morell (Tarragona, Spain), dated in the 3rd century AD. Found in El Morell, 15km from Tarragona, on the ancient road from Tarragona to Lleida. The inscription, wich is incomplete, refers to the restoration carried out by Publius Portus on the road that led from Tarraco to Ilerda in time of Valerian and Gallienus. The Romans placed these mile-stones on the most important communications routes to show the distance in miles between the specific place and the city of Rome. 1206 photos completely processed in Reality Capture. The project was done with the support of the National Archaeological Museum of Tarragona and the Agència Catalana del Patrimoni Cultural. Catalog No. MNAT 37246. Museu Nacional Arqueològic de Tarragona (2019): Tarraco: Exposición de síntesis. Generalitat de Catalunya Publicacions.

sf:ccbe2e02eec74504866e93b26c4516bd.d: Roman marble funerary monument dated in the 3rd century A.D. It belonged to Lucius Julius Polybius as the inscription of four lines that still retains on one of its faces and in which we can read: D(is). M(anibus). S(acrum) L(ucius). I(ulius). POLIBIVS ANN(orum). LXXII (septuaginta duorum) H(ic). S(itus). E(st). S(it). T(ibi). T(erra). L(evis). The translation according to Encarnação, (1984) would say: “Consecrated to the Manes gods. Here lies Lucius Julius Polybius, seventy-two years old. May the earth be light to you”. The funerary monument is of the Cupa type, named for its characteristic cylindrical shape that mimics a lying tank (Cupa means barrel in Latin). It is currently preserved in the Frei Manuel do Cenáculo National Museum (Évora, Portugal). Catalog No. ME1723. sf:cf67bd47903a4a8cb9b6586bacb7d68c.d: This medieval inscription (38 x 21 cm) located in the cathedral of Sigüenza (Spain) says: VITALIS : VITA : SUBLACTUS : SORTE : LEVITA : PRIMUS : IN : HOC : ATRIO : CLAUDITUR : HOSPICIO : ERA : MILLESIMA : DUCENTESIMA : TRICESIMA : PBR : HUNC : SEQUITUR : W. : ET : HIC : SEPELITUR : Vital, por suerte levita, arrebatado de la vida, es el primero que en este claustro recibe albergue en la era 1230 (1192 d.C.). A este le sigue el presbítero W. y aquí esta sepultado. 3D model made in Reality Capture using 200 images with additional processing completed in Geomagic Wrap. This work is part of the collaboration agreement signed in 2020 between the Junta de Comunidades de Castilla-La Mancha and Global Digital Heritage. We want to thank the Bishopric of Sigüenza-Guadalajara and the cathedral chapter, especially D. Jesús de las Heras, D. Miguel Ángel Ortega and D. Julián García, for the facilities and for the interest they have shown in the project.

sf:d0b53a80ebd545a6abe8ad5f23a5ebca.d: This sandstone idol was originally placed in a niche inside a temple. It depicts a stylized face in the Arabian style of Nabataean art. The eyes of the idol were originally inlaid (with semi-precious stones?), while the cavity at the centre of the laurel crown may have contained attributes of the represented goddess. The Nabataean inscription on the base notes who is represented: goddess of Hayyan son of Nayibat. Raqmu-Petra, Temple of the Winged Lions. Nabataean (early 1st century AD). JP13483 . This project was a collaboration between the PDTRA, DoA, GDH, and ACOR. Scanned by GDH in November 2024 using Leo Artec.

sf:d7ea4fa8567448c79e01f0c5db56ef8c.d: A large fragment of a round-topped donation stela of sandstone. The winged disc representing Horus of Behdet (Behdety) is depicted in the lunette. Emanating from the sun disc are two uraei, who wear the White Crown (left) and Red Crown (right). An inscription between them reads "Behdety, the Great God, Lord of the Sky". A pt (sky) sign separates the lunette from the scene below. In this scene, the ruler is depicted on the right side making a donation to a procession of deities. He wears the Double Crown with an uraeus at the front. The cartouches above read pr-ꜥꜣ (Pharaoh) rather than giving the name of the ruler. The procession of gods consists of Montu-Re, Montu-Re-Horakhty, Tjenenet-Iunit, and Raettawy. Both forms of Montu hold a was-sceptre and wear a headdress consisting of double plumes and sun disc. Both have a double uraeus on their forehead. Tjenenet-Iunit wears the Double Crown while holding a papyrus staff, while Raettawy has a headdress consisting of cow horns and a sun disc.

sf:d8a3d415fd764471af8f95895f08c0a8.d: Amulet of the lion-headed goddess Bastet in faience. The goddess has a mane and a tripartite wig. There is a uraeus on the top of her head, which continues into a suspension loop at the back. She is in a striding pose with the right arm at the side while the left one is holding a wadjet eye on the chest. There is a plinth at the bottom. The back pillar carries the hieroglyphic inscription identifying the goddess: ‘Words spoken by Bastet’. The corner of the base is chipped. Previously part of the Ogden collection, which was gifted to Harrogate Museum in the 1930s. Bastet was the feline goddess of female sexuality, pregnant women, and children.

sf:d45c656d5376476ea4e35b60d4d59533.d: An irregular limestone stela, which dates from the Byzantine Period of Egypt (c. fourth to seventh centuries AD). The obverse surface features a deeply incised inscription arranged in at least nine horizontal lines, written in Coptic. Despite some minor surface wear and irregular breaks along the edges of the stone, the text remains legible, preserving standard funerary phrasing dedicated to a monk named Mêna, who belonged to the topos of the venerable Apollô (potentially Bāwīṭ, though other monastic sites are attested). Spelling features point toward Middle Egypt, and Mêna's day of repose is recorded as the tenth of Mešir (corresponding to February 4th or 5th depending on leap years). The reverse side is rough-hewn with visible chisel marks, indicating that the stone was originally embedded into a wall or architectural structure.

sf:e97f95d5781a4359b5a744b0cf0328fa.n: Votive stele - Buddha and two Bodhisattvas
sf:e97f95d5781a4359b5a744b0cf0328fa.d: Buddhist votive stele with Buddha and two Bodhisattvas, 678 CE, now at Mia. From [artsmia.org](www.artsmia.org): *'This stone stele depicts the Buddha sitting on a lotus throne, flanked by a pair of bodhisattvas. His left hand is raised in abhaya mudra (gesture of dispelling fear), and the right is resting on his knee. The figures in this stele illustrate the vivid and naturalistic qualities that are characteristic of Buddhist icons of the Tang dynasty ... The inscription tells us that the stele was commissioned during the reign of Emperor Gaozong in 678, and remarkably lists both the Emperor and the Empress, Wu, as beneficiaries. It was highly unusual for an empress to be included in this way prior to this time, proving her rising power before ultimately becoming the most powerful woman in the Tang dynasty when she became the de facto ruler of China in 690.'* More information [here](https://collections.artsmia.org/art/140016/buddhist-votive-stele-with-buddha-and-two-bodhisattvas-china)

sf:eb3684f933f24df8b4aaa4a23209e786.d: Receipt ? , 0139. In Greek. 6 x 8 cm. **Digital Object provided by Image Delivery Service, Harvard University:** https://ids.lib.harvard.edu/ids/view/4113458?buttons=y

sf:ec32f9a5550f4d3589e58ed6c267d28a.d: An irregularly shaped limestone stela with a rough, jagged outline, whose front surface features a deeply incised and poorly preserved raised relief carving. The scene depicts two people facing right: a soldier at the front holding a bow in his left hand and a sheaf of arrows in his right, and wearing a broad collar; and behind him, a woman in a long dress with her left arm raised towards the man's head in a gesture of affection or protection. The decoration is executed in a crudely cut style, and faint traces of hieroglyphs are visible above the woman's head. The reverse side is rough and undecorated. This type of stela, known as a "soldier stela", is characteristic of the First Intermediate Period (c. 2181–2055 BC). Purchased by Sir Henry Wellcome in 1906 from the collection of Robert de Rustafjaell. On long-term loan to the Egypt Centre since 1971 as part of the dispersal of the Wellcome collection.

sf:ed9b87c8df9340b4ba691ddc2a8e7daf.n: Funerary inscription of the Spurius family
sf:ed9b87c8df9340b4ba691ddc2a8e7daf.d: Funerary inscription of the Spurius family. Roman, 2nd century BCE. Marble, pigment; 35 x 34.5 x 8 cm. ID: 0000.00.1037. This tombstone for the Spurius family is a rare example of a Republican-period inscription from the Bay of Naples, but it shows some facets that became standardized in later tombstones. The grouping of relatives together in a large tomb was a common practice to demonstrate the family’s wealth, especially if it was in a prominent location. Intriguingly, this inscription was carved on a re-used column base, one of numerous examples of the re-use of building materials for inscriptions and vice-versa. Translation: "Gnaeus Spurius, the son of Ovus; Singullia, the daughter of Marcus; Marcus Spurius, the son of Gnaeus; Gnaeus Spurius, the son of Gnaeus Frugus." For more info and links to raw data, see: https://quod.lib.umich.edu/k/kelsey/x-0000.00.1037

sf:efa0fa04da23480f82baa263d54858ee.d: Headrest New Kingdom Wood Possibly from Illahun Harvard Semitic Museum 1902.17.7 The inscription on column of headrest, starts with “the good god” then a break over what was a cartouche, and ends with “given life.” The cartouche has enough space and traces of inscription to accommodate three or four signs. The last sign appears to be a neb basket, with a seated deity over it (Amenhotep III? Ramses IV?). There is also a (secondarily carved?) sa sign carved on one side of the base, the word for “son” or the god Geb. wear pattern on the cartouche suggests it was grabbed frequently around the post of the headrest, the object may have been used in life and then deposited in a burial. References: Flinders Petrie, Objects of Daily Use (London, 1927), p. 35 no. 32 and pl. XXXII no. 32. sf:f53bc35f3d774f11a9476bfdadae94f7.d: Carl Menger, one of Austria’s most influential economists, is buried in an honorary grave at Vienna Central Cemetery, Group 0, Row 1, Grave 88. The monument is restrained and architectural in design: two stone pillars support a broad upper block bearing the simple inscription “CARL MENGER”. His life dates, 1840–1921, are shown in Roman numerals on the central slab. Small wreath reliefs add discreet decoration to the otherwise austere memorial. The grave monument is attributed to the Austrian sculptor and medallist Richard Ruepp. Menger was born on 23 February 1840 in Neu Sandez, Galicia, today Nowy Sącz in Poland. After studying law, he increasingly turned to economics. His 1871 book Principles of Economics laid the foundations of the Austrian School of Economics. Menger argued that value depends on the importance individuals attach to goods in satisfying their needs. He later became professor at the University of Vienna and also taught Crown Prince Rudolf. Carl Menger died in Vienna on 26 February 1921.

sf:f975e1e56d6744cfb5963367b0160253.d: A complete mummiform wooden shabti dating to the late Eighteenth Dynasty (c. 1400–1300 BC), inscribed for the scribe Nedjem. The figure is carved from wood, with its arms crossed right over left across the chest. Little of the original paint remains across the darkened wooden surface, except for seven rows of black hieroglyphs on the front that record Chapter 6 of the Book of the Dead (the "shabti spell"). Notably, the face and hands contain traces of ancient gilding, adding a costly and reflective element to the facial features and crossed fists. A deep, natural vertical split in the wood runs down the entire left side of the figure, with another significant fissure extending down the centre of the reverse.

sf:f1828f935e8d47d6933f00d8cafb4720.d: Fragment of inscription of a chief magistrate. Roman, Flavian (69–96 CE). Marble, plaster, pigment; 21 x 18.7 x 3.7 cm. ID: 0000.00.0818d. Portion of a monumental public inscription preserving one letter and an interpunct (a dot separating letters and/or words in ancient inscriptions). The edge to the left of the "A." is straight and the back shows possible traces of attachment, suggesting that it is the beginning of the entire inscription. This would leave the "A." standing on its own, suggesting it may be part of a name: "A." was the standard abbreviation of "Aulus", a common Roman praenomen (given/first name). The break on this stone connects with other pieces in our collection, helping to confirm our reading of this fragment. Full inscription: * Latin: *A(ulus) Caeci(lius Ru)fus II vir.* * Translation: "Aulus Caecilius Rufus, the chief magistrate (*duumvir*)." For more info and links to raw data, see: https://quod.lib.umich.edu/k/kelsey/x-0000.00.0818d

sf:f14466adf0c647f48d57a5e96b7696f9.d: This limestone altar has 6 lines of Latin inscribed on two sides. The text mentions Marcus Aurelius Antoninus. (M.AVR. ANTONI), the Roman Emperor from AD 161 to 180. After the annexation of the Nabataean Kingdom into the Roman Empire, Latin - the official language of the Roman Empire - was used in Petra alongside the local Nabataean; Greek also continued to be used. Latin was used for official monument, milestones of the Via Nova Traina and tomb inscriptions of the Romans, like the Latin inscription of the Sextius Florentinus Tomb. This altar was possibly used by the Roman official in Petra. Roman period (AD 161-180). JP6493. This project was a collaboration between the PDTRA, DoA, GDH, and ACOR. Scanned by GDH in November 2024 using Leo Artec scanner.

sf:fbbf72c144da4eec85fbb66cf2800b83.n: Roman Stela from Hardomlje near Ljubuški
sf:fbbf72c144da4eec85fbb66cf2800b83.d: Roman tombstone / Stela with figural decoration and inscription. From Hardomlje near Ljubuški, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Curated in the National Museum, Sarajevo. Data were collected as part of a joint research project between GDH and the Association for the Digitization and Informatisation of Cultural Heritage (DIGI.BA) in Sarajevo, in full collaboration with the National Museum of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sarajevo. Model was created from 422 images from a Canon 5D mk IV. All data were processed in Reality Capture. Project ID NMB RomanTomstone4.

sf:fbdbac87b671468ebea9fc8f2166482a.n: Funerary inscription of a Praetorian officer
sf:fbdbac87b671468ebea9fc8f2166482a.d: Funerary inscription of Lucius Calpurnius Rufus. Roman, 71–214 CE. Marble; 29 x 38 x 2.6 cm. ID: 0000.00.0878. The Praetorian fleet at Misenum was founded by Augustus in 27 BCE and protected the western Mediterranean from piracy and other naval threats. Lucius Calpurnius Rufus was a scriba—an administrative role within the navy that would serve as a ship or squadron’s clerk—for this fleet. This inscription was set up in Italy, even though he passed away and was buried in Ephesus (Türkiye). This inscription was written on the back of a reused fragment of a monumental inscription, probably Augustan in date. Translation: "To the Shades of the Underworld: for Lucius Calpurnius Rufus, an officer (scriba) of the Praetorian fleet of Misenum. This man, sent to Ephesus on duty, died and was laid there in a marble sarcophagus. Marcus Sittius Africanus, his fellow countryman and heir, made this memorial at the camp." For more info and links to raw data, see: https://quod.lib.umich.edu/k/kelsey/x-0000.00.0878
